concepts.title: Degree and Cardinality of a Relation

questions.q: Using the method 'Degree and Cardinality of a Relation', work with: attrs = 25, tuples = 360. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of nonkey_cells.
questions.a: 8640 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Degree and Cardinality of a Relation' and work with: attrs = 40, tuples = 240. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of nonkey_cells.
questions.a: 9360 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Degree and Cardinality of a Relation' refers to.
questions.a: In a relation, the degree counts its attributes (columns) and the cardinality counts its tuples (rows); multiplying the two gives the number of data values the relation state holds, of which one column per row is usually the key.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Degree and Cardinality of a Relation'.
questions.a: The GUARDIAN relation of Figure 8.4 has degree 4 and cardinality 5, so it stores 20 values.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Degree and Cardinality of a Relation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: cells = attrs * tuples

questions.q: Using the method 'Attendance Percentage from Working Days', work with: present_days = 24, working_days = 12. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of percent.
questions.a: 200 per cent

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Attendance Percentage from Working Days' and work with: present_days = 240, working_days = 18. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of percent.
questions.a: 1333.3333 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Attendance Percentage from Working Days' refers to.
questions.a: A school consolidates attendance by dividing the days a student was marked present by the total working days and scaling to percent, which is the calculation done manually in registers but reliably by software.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Attendance Percentage from Working Days'.
questions.a: In the ATTENDANCE snapshot, roll number 3 is absent on both dates, so the percentage is 0.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Attendance Percentage from Working Days', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: percent = present_days / working_days * 100

questions.q: How many attendance records must a teacher write each month for a class of 50 over 26 working days? Use the method 'Manual Register Record Count'. Work with: days = 5, students = 25. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of yearly_entries.
questions.a: 1500 years

questions.q: Compute the yearly attendance entries for the same class.. Use the method 'Manual Register Record Count'. Work with: days = 500, students = 50. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of yearly_entries.
questions.a: 300000 years

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Manual Register Record Count' refers to.
questions.a: The chapter opens by counting the burden of paper registers: a class of 50 students over 26 working days needs 50 times 26 entries every month, and the yearly total shows why manual entry becomes tedious.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Manual Register Record Count'.
questions.a: Fifty students across 26 working days produce 1300 attendance records in one month.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Manual Register Record Count', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: yearly_entries = students * days * 12

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Limitations of the File System' refers to.
questions.a: Storing data in separate files brings trouble: access needs custom programs, the same data get duplicated (redundancy), duplicated copies drift apart (inconsistency), related files stay unlinked (isolation), format changes break programs (dependence), and fine-grained sharing is hard to enforce.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Limitations of the File System'.
questions.a: Student names appear in both STUDENT and ATTENDANCE files, so a spelling change must be made twice or the files disagree.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Limitations of the File System', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: redundancy -> inconsistency -> extra storage and errors

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Database Management System Basics' refers to.
questions.a: A DBMS is software that creates and manages databases, serving as the interface between users and stored data; its key terms are schema (the design), constraints, metadata or data dictionary, instance (a snapshot of the state), query, data manipulation and the database engine.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Database Management System Basics'.
questions.a: The DBMS keeps one centralised repository that the teacher and office staff can query at the same time.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Database Management System Basics', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: query -> DBMS -> database -> query result

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Attribute, Tuple and Domain' refers to.
questions.a: Relational vocabulary: a column of a relation is an attribute (also called field), a row is a tuple representing one entity's facts, and the domain is the set of permitted values for an attribute, such as integers for RollNumber or strings for SName.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Attribute, Tuple and Domain'.
questions.a: GUID, GName, GPhone and GAddress are the four attributes of relation GUARDIAN.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Attribute, Tuple and Domain', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: relation = attributes (columns) x tuples (rows), values from domains

concepts.title: Candidate, Primary, Composite and Foreign Keys

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Candidate, Primary, Composite and Foreign Keys' refers to.
questions.a: Keys enforce tuple uniqueness and relationships: attributes that can uniquely identify tuples are candidate keys; the designer's chosen candidate becomes the primary key and the rest are alternate keys; two or more attributes can form a composite primary key; and a foreign key in one relation refers to the primary key of another to link them.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Candidate, Primary, Composite and Foreign Keys'.
questions.a: In GUARDIAN, GUID and GPhone are candidate keys; choosing GUID as primary makes GPhone the alternate key.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Candidate, Primary, Composite and Foreign Keys', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: {RollNumber, AttendanceDate} -> composite primary key of ATTENDANCE

concepts.title: Properties of a Relation and NULL

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Properties of a Relation and NULL' refers to.
questions.a: A relation differs from a plain table by three properties: attribute names are unique and their order immaterial, every tuple is distinct and unordered, and each value is atomic, from one domain, single-valued, with NULL marking unknown or inapplicable values.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Properties of a Relation and NULL'.
questions.a: A guardian who withholds a phone number gets NULL under GPhone rather than a fake number.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Properties of a Relation and NULL', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: no duplicate tuples; atomic single-domain values; NULL = unknown
